questions.question: The 472–479 kHz amateur allocation is described as secondary. Which service is the primary user of this spectrum?
options: The Ministry of Defence, operating fixed military communication networks
Maritime mobile services, including ship-to-shore communication
Aeronautical navigation aids, including NDB beacons
Broadcast services — medium-wave AM radio stations
questions.explanation: The 472–479 kHz band is allocated to maritime mobile services as the primary user; amateur radio has secondary status. This means amateurs must not cause interference to maritime stations and must accept any interference from them. The wavelength is approximately 630 metres — it is often called the 630 m band.

questions.question: What is the general maximum EIRP permitted for amateur operation on the 472–479 kHz band?
options: 100 W EIRP — the same limit that applies on most HF bands
10 W EIRP — the standard secondary-allocation power ceiling
5 W EIRP — the general limit for the 630 m band
1 W EIRP — the limit that applies regardless of station location
questions.explanation: The general maximum EIRP on 472–479 kHz is 5 W. A reduced limit of 1 W EIRP applies when your station is within 800 km of certain specified neighbouring countries, irrespective of whether those countries' stations are actually active on the frequency. The 1 W limit is geographic, not reciprocal.

questions.question: On the 5 MHz amateur slots, which organisation holds primary user status that amateur stations must not interfere with?
options: GCHQ — UK signals intelligence, operating fixed-frequency monitoring receivers
The Ministry of Defence — military services operating across the 5 MHz range
Ofcom — who runs a national frequency monitoring network on 5 MHz
Maritime Coastguard Agency — operating distress and safety channels
questions.explanation: The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is the primary user of the 5 MHz range in the UK. Amateur radio is granted secondary status in narrow channel slots across 5.2585–5.4065 MHz, strictly on a non-interference basis. The MoD actively uses these frequencies, so operating outside your licensed slot or causing interference has real consequences.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the structure of the 5 MHz amateur allocation?
options: A single continuous block of 200 kHz, centred on 5.350 MHz, available 24 hours a day
Three contiguous sub-bands (CW, SSB, and digital) spanning 5.250–5.450 MHz
A set of individual narrow channel slots spread across the range 5.2585–5.4065 MHz
A shared frequency at exactly 5.300 MHz with access on a first-come first-served basis
questions.explanation: Unlike conventional amateur bands, 5 MHz is allocated as a collection of individual narrow channel slots within the range 5.2585–5.4065 MHz — not a continuous block. The slots vary in width and are interspersed with MoD frequencies. Before operating, you must consult the current band plan in the EX309 Reference Booklet, as slot assignments are subject to change as MoD use evolves.

questions.question: You are using a two-tone digital mode on a 5 MHz slot. Both your audio tones fall within the slot boundaries, but the upper tone is just 50 Hz below the upper slot edge. Your rig's USB passband extends a further 200 Hz above the upper tone. Is your transmission within the slot?
options: No — the upper edge of the USB passband extends outside the slot, breaching the 5 MHz condition
Yes — only the transmitted carriers and tones must fall within the slot; the rig's passband width is irrelevant
Yes — a 50 Hz margin is sufficient regardless of audio passband width
No — all digital modes on 5 MHz must use tones below 500 Hz audio offset from the dial frequency
questions.explanation: The 5 MHz condition requires that all transmitted carriers or tones fall wholly within the allocated slot. What matters is where your actual transmitted energy lies — the rig's nominal SSB audio passband width is not the test; the test is whether your tones are within the slot. In this scenario, both tones are inside the slot, so the transmission complies. Use a waterfall display to verify in practice.

questions.question: Which of the following contacts is explicitly permitted on the 5 MHz band, despite the usual amateur-to-amateur-only convention?
options: Contacts with CB (Citizens Band) radio operators during an emergency
Contacts with licensed broadcast engineers coordinating frequency use
Contacts with military personnel and military cadets operating on 5 MHz
Contacts with Ofcom spectrum monitoring staff during a compliance inspection
questions.explanation: Because the MoD is the primary user of 5 MHz, contact with military personnel and military cadets is explicitly permitted on this band. Military stations may legitimately want to exchange communications with amateur stations, and the 5 MHz allocation recognises this reality. The exception applies specifically to 5 MHz — the normal restriction on contacting non-amateur stations applies everywhere else.

questions.question: You are operating on 472 kHz with a transmitter output of 50 W. Your antenna system has a feed efficiency of 4% (i.e. the antenna radiates 4% of the power delivered to it). Your station is 900 km from the nearest specified neighbouring country. What is your EIRP, and are you within the applicable limit?
options: EIRP = 50 W; exceeds the 5 W limit — you must reduce transmitter power
EIRP = 2 W; exceeds the 1 W limit because you are within 800 km of a specified country
EIRP = 2 W; within the 5 W general limit because your station is more than 800 km from any specified country
EIRP = 2 W; within the 1 W reduced limit because antenna efficiency losses always count toward compliance
questions.explanation: EIRP = transmitter output × antenna system efficiency = 50 W × 4% = 2 W. Because your station is 900 km from the nearest specified neighbouring country — which is more than 800 km — the reduced 1 W limit does not apply. The general limit is 5 W EIRP, and 2 W is well within this. This illustrates why you must calculate actual EIRP from the antenna system rather than assuming EIRP equals transmitter output: at 472 kHz, a short antenna's efficiency losses may be large enough to keep EIRP well below the limit even at moderate transmitter power.

questions.question: A rare DX station announces it is 'listening 5 to 10 up'. You want to call it. Where should you set your transmit VFO?
options: On the DX station's transmit frequency, so you can be sure you are on the right channel
5 to 10 kHz below the DX transmit frequency, as 'up' refers to the DX station moving up
5 to 10 kHz above the DX station's transmit frequency
Anywhere in the amateur band — the DX station will scan the whole band for callers
questions.explanation: In split operation, the DX station transmits on its published frequency and listens for callers somewhere 5 to 10 kHz higher in the band. 'Listening 5 to 10 up' means the listening range is 5 to 10 kHz above the DX transmit frequency. You must set your transmit VFO — not your receive VFO — into that range. Calling on the DX transmit frequency means transmitting where nobody is listening, and will annoy every operator trying to copy the DX.

questions.question: You are working a DX pileup in split mode, transmitting 7 kHz above the DX station's published frequency. The DX keeps responding to stations but never to you, even though your signal report on other bands is good. What is the most likely cause and appropriate action?
options: Your transmitter output is probably too high — reduce power to avoid overloading the DX receiver
You may be outside the portion of the listening range the DX is currently favouring — move your transmit frequency up or down within the 5–10 kHz range
The DX station is probably only working stations from a particular continent — try again at a different time of day
You should call on the DX transmit frequency once to attract attention, then move back to split
questions.explanation: The DX station may not be scanning its entire 5–10 kHz listening range uniformly. If it is currently picking up callers at the top of that range and you are transmitting at 7 kHz up, you may be in a less-favoured part of the spread. Listen carefully to where the stations the DX does reply to are transmitting, and adjust your frequency accordingly — within the announced listening range. Never call on the DX transmit frequency.

questions.question: You have two HF transceivers. You want to transmit on one while monitoring the DX station on the other, with both rigs connected to antennas in your garden a few metres apart. What risk does this create?
options: Ofcom may classify this as operating two simultaneous amateur stations, which requires a second licence
The transmitted RF from one rig may couple into the other rig's receive antenna, potentially damaging or desensitising its front end
ICNIRP EMF field strengths will double because two antennas are radiating, requiring a fresh compliance assessment
The two rigs will produce intermodulation products on your transmit frequency, causing spurious emissions
questions.explanation: When you transmit on one rig while a second rig is listening on a nearby frequency, the transmitted RF can couple into the second antenna and overwhelm or damage the second receiver's front-end. The two antennas are physically close, so isolation is poor. To avoid this you need either adequate physical antenna separation or remote operation with one antenna at a different location.

questions.question: A DX station announces: 'QRZ, listening 14.225 to 14.230'. You set your transmit VFO to 14.227 MHz and call twice. The DX replies 'M0 — something', suggesting it is working an M0 station. You cannot copy the station being worked at all. What does this situation most likely indicate, and what is the best response?
options: The DX station has poor ears — increase power to the maximum permitted level and call more frequently
You are on the correct transmit frequency; the problem is that your signal report is poor — switch to a higher-gain antenna
The station the DX worked may have better propagation or antenna advantage; your path is marginal — continue calling patiently in the published listening range, adjusting frequency if necessary
You should move your transmit frequency to 14.225 MHz exactly — the DX always works stations at the bottom of its announced range
questions.explanation: Not being able to copy the stations the DX is working is a sign of a path disadvantage — perhaps a directional antenna pointed away from your region, or propagation that favours another continent. This is a normal feature of HF pileups. The appropriate response is to continue calling patiently in the correct listening range, adjusting your transmit frequency systematically to find where the DX is picking up callers. Increasing power beyond the licence limit is not permitted; moving outside the published listening range is counterproductive.

questions.question: Why does a DX station use split frequency operation rather than asking callers to call on the same frequency it transmits on?
options: To comply with IARU band plan recommendations that prohibit DX stations from receiving on their own transmit frequency
Because calling stations transmitting on the DX frequency would produce a solid wall of overlapping signals that the DX cannot separate — split spreads the callers across a wider frequency range
To prevent interference to the DX station's own transmitted signal by keeping callers at least 5 kHz away
To allow Ofcom to identify and log the calling stations separately from the DX entity being contacted
questions.explanation: When many stations call on a single frequency simultaneously, the signals overlap and become unintelligible — the DX station hears a continuous roar. By asking callers to spread themselves across a 5–10 kHz listening range, the DX station can pick out individual signals that are separated in frequency. Split operation is a practical technique to manage high-demand contacts, not a regulatory requirement.

questions.question: You hear an amateur station transmitting on a frequency that does not appear in the UK licence schedule. Are you permitted to listen, and may you reply?
options: You may neither listen nor reply — monitoring frequencies outside your schedule is not permitted
You may listen freely but may only reply on a frequency within your UK licence schedule
You may listen and reply on the same frequency, provided the contact is brief and you return to a UK frequency immediately afterwards
You may reply only if the station is in CEPT country and you are operating under T/R 61-01
questions.explanation: There is no restriction on listening to amateur transmissions on any frequency — reception is unrestricted. However, your transmit obligations remain tied to your UK licence schedule. You may only transmit on frequencies listed in that schedule. If an overseas station wants to contact UK stations specifically, they will choose a frequency or indicate a listening frequency within the UK schedule.

questions.question: You are running a net and invite a station from a country with a tiered licence system to respond. The station replies on your net frequency, which is within their country's Full-equivalent allocation. Later you discover the station holds only their country's entry-level licence and is not permitted on that frequency. Who bears responsibility for the breach?
options: You, the net control — you should have verified every station's licence class before permitting them to transmit
The overseas station — they alone are responsible for operating within their own national licence conditions
The ITU — they should harmonise tiered licence access across all regions to prevent this situation
Shared equally between you and the overseas station — net control has a duty of care to all participants
questions.explanation: Each licensed amateur is individually responsible for complying with the licence conditions under which they operate. An overseas station that transmits on a frequency their tier does not permit is in breach of their own national regulations — that is their regulatory responsibility, not yours. As net control you cannot realistically verify the licence tier of every station. The key learning point is that just because you can hear a station on a frequency does not mean they are legally permitted to reply there.

questions.question: When operating abroad under CEPT T/R 61-01, you find that the host country's band plan places the SSB calling frequency on 14.150 MHz — 25 kHz below where the IARU Region 1 plan recommends. Which frequency plan must you follow?
options: The IARU Region 1 band plan — it takes precedence over national deviations in all CEPT countries
Whichever plan gives you access to the largest portion of the band — this is at your discretion
The host country's band plan and national licence conditions — T/R 61-01 requires you to follow host country rules
The UK band plan — your UK licence conditions apply even when operating abroad under T/R 61-01
questions.explanation: CEPT T/R 61-01 requires visiting operators to comply with the host country's national licence conditions and band plans. IARU band plans are recommendations — national administrations may deviate from them, and where they do, the national plan governs. Operating under T/R 61-01 means you are treated as if you hold that country's Full licence, so you must follow their rules.

questions.question: An overseas amateur station contacts you and says they are listening on 7.100 MHz but transmitting to you from 7.060 MHz, which is outside the UK amateur band plan sub-band for that mode. You are in the UK on your UK licence. What constraints govern your reply, and on which frequency may you transmit?
options: You must reply on 7.060 MHz to match the overseas station's transmit frequency — operating simplex is required once you have established contact
You may transmit only on frequencies within your UK licence schedule that are appropriate for the mode — you cannot follow the overseas station to 7.060 MHz if that is outside the UK schedule
You may transmit on 7.060 MHz because the overseas station's use of that frequency confirms it is internationally allocated
You must first obtain an NoV from Ofcom to operate outside the standard UK band plan sub-band allocations
questions.explanation: Your transmit frequency is always governed by your UK licence schedule. If 7.060 MHz is outside the frequencies permitted to you in the UK schedule for the mode and band in question, you may not transmit there — even to respond to a station that is transmitting from that frequency. The overseas station will already be aware of this constraint if they have called you on your listening frequency (7.100 MHz in this example), which is within the UK schedule. You reply on a frequency within your UK allocation.

questions.section_name: Callsign Suffixes, Special Event Stations, and Supervising
questions.question: You drive to a hilltop and set up your amateur station for a portable activation. You are not in a moving vehicle; the site is not your main or alternative registered address. Which suffix should you append to your callsign?
options: /M — mobile, because you drove to the location
/A — alternative address, because you are away from home
/P — portable, because you are at a fixed temporary site that is not a registered address
/MM — maritime mobile, because you are operating in the open air
questions.explanation: /P (portable) is the correct suffix for operation from a fixed temporary site that is neither your main station address nor a registered alternative address — a hilltop activation is the classic example. /M is used when actually mobile (in a vehicle or on foot). /A denotes a registered alternative premises. /MM is for maritime mobile operation at sea.

questions.section_name: Callsign Suffixes, Special Event Stations, and Supervising
questions.question: A special event station with the callsign GB0HRY is on the air at a heritage railway event. Which document authorises the use of this callsign in place of the organiser's normal callsign?
options: A Club Station licence issued directly to the heritage railway society by Ofcom
A Notice of Variation (NoV) attached to the organising Full licence holder's existing licence
A temporary operating permit issued by the RSGB Events Committee
A reciprocal licence issued to the heritage railway under the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006
questions.explanation: Special event callsigns are authorised by a Notice of Variation (NoV) issued by Ofcom. The NoV is a modification of an existing Full licence, not a separate licence. The Full licence holder operating under the NoV remains legally responsible for all transmissions under the event callsign, exactly as though they were using their own personal callsign.

questions.section_name: Callsign Suffixes, Special Event Stations, and Supervising
questions.question: You are a Full licence holder supervising an unlicensed trainee who is operating your station. During the contact, the trainee uses a different callsign they found online, believing it is 'more suitable for the contact'. What is the correct procedure, and what are the licensing implications?
options: The trainee may use any callsign provided it is a valid UK amateur callsign — the licence does not require the supervisor's own callsign to be used
The trainee must stop transmitting immediately; only your callsign may be used, and you as Full licensee are responsible for correcting the breach
The trainee may use a training callsign (e.g. M3-prefix) issued for trainee use under supervised operation
You should QSY to a different frequency and resume the contact using your callsign — the previous transmission becomes void
questions.explanation: An unlicensed operator under Full licence supervision must use the Full licensee's own callsign — no other callsign is permitted. There is no trainee callsign designation. The Full licensee is legally responsible for all transmissions from their station during supervised operation, including the breach caused by using an unauthorised callsign. You must correct the error immediately and ensure only your callsign is used going forward.

questions.section_name: Callsign Suffixes, Special Event Stations, and Supervising
questions.question: A Full licence holder sets up their station at a friend's house and leaves an unlicensed friend to continue transmitting while they go to the kitchen for 30 minutes, saying 'you'll be fine — just talk to people'. The friend makes several transmissions that, unknown to the licence holder, contain prohibited content. Which statement best describes the regulatory position?
options: The friend is solely responsible — the licence holder cannot be held responsible for transmissions made in their absence
Neither party is responsible — prohibited content transmitted in good faith by an unlicensed person is a regulatory grey area
The Full licence holder is legally responsible for all the transmissions made during their absence and faces the regulatory consequences, because active supervision was not maintained
The Full licence holder is only responsible for the transmissions they were physically present to hear
questions.explanation: Supervision of an unlicensed operator requires active oversight — not merely being in the same building or nearby. Leaving an unlicensed person to transmit unmonitored for 30 minutes does not constitute direct supervision. The Full licence holder remains legally responsible for every transmission made from their station under their licence during that period, as if they had made those transmissions themselves. This includes any prohibited content. The consequence (warning, licence variation, or revocation) falls on the Full licensee.
